title: Secure the Lambda Handler
objective: Review a Lambda handler that feeds event data into a shell command, a SQL query and a file path, fix it with validation and safe APIs, prove the fix with a scan and tests, and shrink the function's execution role to least privilege.
successCriteria: You identified the three unsafe sinks (shell, SQL, filesystem path) in the handler
You chose the rewrite that removes the shell and validates input, and the static-analysis gate passes
You rewrote the execution role to one bucket prefix plus its own log group
hints: Follow the data: which values come from the event, and which interpreter (shell, database, filesystem) receives them?
Prefer designs where input is data and never instructions: allow-lists, argument lists with shell=False, bound query parameters.

Apply option B with ./apply-fix.sh B, run pytest -q, then bandit -r handler.py -ll. For the role, allow only GetObject/PutObject on the exports/ prefix plus CreateLogStream/PutLogEvents on the function's own log group.

range.scenario: You are the security engineer reviewing report-exporter, a Lambda function behind an internal API in account 111122223333. It takes a report name and a customer name from the query string, archives a report folder, looks up the customer's orders and publishes the archive to S3. A teammate wants it in production this week. Review the code and the function's role, fix what you find, and prove the fix with the team's static-analysis scan and unit tests. Everything here is a simulation with fictional resources; you only inspect, fix and verify.

artifacts.content:
import os
import sqlite3
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
db = sqlite3.connect("/tmp/orders.db")


def handler(event, context):
    params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}
    report = params.get("report", "")
    customer = params.get("customer", "")

    # 1. archive the requested report folder
    os.system("tar czf /tmp/" + report + ".tgz /var/task/reports/" + report)

    # 2. look up the customer's orders
    cur = db.cursor()
    cur.execute("SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer = '%s'" % customer)
    rows = cur.fetchall()

    # 3. read a previously exported CSV for the same report name
    with open("/tmp/exports/" + report + ".csv") as f:
        csv_data = f.read()

    # 4. publish the archive and confirm the upload
    with open("/tmp/" + report + ".tgz", "rb") as f:
        s3.put_object(Bucket=os.environ["REPORT_BUCKET"], Key="exports/" + report + ".tgz", Body=f)
    s3.get_object(Bucket=os.environ["REPORT_BUCKET"], Key="exports/" + report + ".tgz")

    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": csv_data}

tasks.prompt: Review handler.py. Which lines build a shell command, a query or a filesystem path directly out of values taken from the event? Select all that apply.
options: os.system(...) built by concatenating the report name from the event into a command string
cur.execute(...) building the SQL text with % formatting of the customer value
open("/tmp/exports/" + report + ".csv") with a filename taken from the event
s3 = boto3.client("s3") created once at module scope
params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {} reading the query string
tasks.explanation: The three sinks are a shell (os.system), a query engine (cursor.execute) and the filesystem (open). In each, text that came from the caller is mixed into an instruction that another interpreter will parse. Creating the client at module scope is a normal Lambda performance pattern, and merely reading the event is fine: the danger starts where unvalidated data reaches a sink.

tasks.prompt: In Python's subprocess module, which keyword argument (written as name=value) hands the command string to /bin/sh for parsing, and so must be avoided with event data?
tasks.explanation: With shell=True (and with os.system, which always uses a shell) the whole string is parsed by the shell, so metacharacters in the data become shell syntax. Passing an argument list with shell=False runs the program directly and every list item is one literal argument, so the data cannot change the command's structure.

tasks.prompt: Pick the safest rewrite for step 1 (archiving the report). Remember its letter: the terminal's ./apply-fix.sh applies your chosen option so you can verify it with the scanner and the tests.
options: Option A: strip the characters ; & | from report, then keep os.system(...)
Option B: check report against an allow-list of known report names, then run subprocess.run(["tar", "czf", out_path, src_path], shell=False)
Option C: wrap the value with shlex.quote(report) and keep subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)
Option D: keep os.system(...) but wrap it in try/except and return a generic 500 error
tasks.explanation: Option B removes the shell from the path entirely and restricts the input to values you expect (validate against an allow-list, do not try to remove bad characters). A and C keep a shell in the loop and depend on a block-list or quoting being perfect; D hides errors but changes nothing about what runs. Prefer 'no interpreter at all' over 'sanitise and hope'.

tasks.prompt: Which change correctly fixes step 2, the customer lookup?
options: cur.execute("SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer = ?", (customer,)) with a bound parameter
Replace each single quote in customer with two single quotes before formatting it in
Reject the request if customer contains the words SELECT, UNION or DROP
Switch from % formatting to an f-string
tasks.explanation: A parameterized query sends the SQL text and the value separately, so the value is always treated as data (the name O'Brien just works). Hand-rolled escaping, keyword block-lists and a different string-formatting style all still build the query text from the input and break on edge cases.

tasks.prompt: In the terminal: inspect the function and its role, run the scan to see the findings, apply your chosen fix with ./apply-fix.sh <letter>, confirm the tests pass with benign inputs, then re-run the scan until the gate passes. Paste the release token it prints.
tasks.explanation: The first scan reports the shell and SQL findings; after the fix the scan is clean and the unit tests (including a customer named O'Brien and an unknown report name) pass. Scanning, testing and gating on every change is how you keep these patterns from coming back.

tasks.prompt: The function's execution role report-exporter-role is far broader than the handler needs. Rewrite the policy for least privilege: the function reads and writes objects only under the exports/ prefix of the acme-reports-prod bucket, and writes logs only to its own log group (/aws/lambda/report-exporter) in us-east-1, account 111122223333.

tests.name: Can write exports to the exports/ prefix
Can read exports from the exports/ prefix
Cannot read other prefixes in the same bucket
Cannot delete exported objects
Cannot list every bucket in the account
Can write to its own log group
Cannot write to another function's log group
Cannot pass a role to another service

tasks.explanation: Even a perfectly fixed handler should not run with s3:* and logs:* on every resource, because the next bug in this function would inherit all of it. Scope actions to what the code calls (GetObject and PutObject), resources to one bucket prefix and one log group, and leave out everything else: anything not allowed is implicitly denied.

tasks.prompt: The code is now fixed. Why is it still worth shrinking the execution role?
options: Defence in depth: if a similar bug appears later, the blast radius is limited to what the role can do
Because a smaller role makes the Lambda function run faster
Because Lambda refuses to invoke functions whose roles use wildcards
It is not worth it once static analysis passes
tasks.explanation: Static analysis and tests reduce the chance of a flaw, but they cannot prove there are none. A least-privilege role limits what any future flaw (or a vulnerable dependency) can reach. Permissions do not affect speed, and Lambda happily runs wildcard roles, which is exactly why you must review them yourself.

takeaways: Untrusted event data must never reach a shell, a query or a filesystem path unvalidated: use allow-lists, argument lists with shell=False and bound query parameters.
Remove the dangerous interpreter rather than trying to sanitise around it: quoting and block-lists are fragile.
Back every fix with a scan and tests, and keep the execution role least-privilege so the next bug has a small blast radius.

title: Right-Size a Lambda Execution Role
objective: Use an IAM Access Analyzer unused-access report and the function's code to right-size an over-permissive Lambda execution role, apply the least-privilege policy, and verify the function still works.
successCriteria: You used the unused-access report to identify permissions that can be removed
You rewrote the role to one bucket prefix, one secret, one table and its own logs, with no iam:PassRole
The function still works and the re-check reports no active unused-access findings
hints: Start with the analyzer: list the analyzers, list the findings, then read the finding details for the role.
Compare the report with processor.py. Keep only what the code calls, on the exact resources it touches, and treat the report as a signal to verify rather than a verdict.

Allow s3:GetObject/PutObject on invoices/*, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the one secret ARN, dynamodb:GetItem/PutItem/Query on the one table ARN and the two log actions; drop iam:PassRole entirely.

range.scenario: You own the invoice-processor Lambda function in account 111122223333. It was built under deadline and its execution role was given s3:*, secretsmanager:*, dynamodb:* and iam:PassRole on every resource 'to make it work'. A quarterly review flags the role as high risk. Your account has an IAM Access Analyzer configured for unused access with a 90-day window. Use the report together with the function's code to decide what the role really needs, rewrite it, and prove the function still works. Everything here is simulated with fictional resources.

artifacts.content:
import os
import boto3

BUCKET = "acme-invoices-prod"
SECRET_ID = "prod/invoice-api-key"

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
secrets = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("invoices")


def handler(event, context):
    key = event["detail"]["object"]["key"]            # always invoices/<file>.pdf

    pdf = s3.get_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=key)["Body"].read()
    api_key = secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId=SECRET_ID)["SecretString"]

    invoice = extract_fields(pdf, api_key)             # calls the OCR vendor API

    if not table.get_item(Key={"invoice_id": invoice["id"]}).get("Item"):
        table.put_item(Item=invoice)
    table.query(
        IndexName=None,
        KeyConditionExpression="invoice_id = :i",
        ExpressionAttributeValues={":i": invoice["id"]},
    )

    s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key="invoices/processed/" + invoice["id"] + ".json", Body=str(invoice))
    return {"status": "processed", "invoice": invoice["id"]}

tasks.prompt: Use the terminal to list the unused-access analyzer, its findings and the finding details for invoice-processor-role. Which service namespace shows no last-accessed time at all (nothing in that service was used in the whole 90-day window)?
tasks.explanation: Every other service in the finding has a lastAccessed time because the function really does call it, but the iam entry has none: the function has never used its iam:PassRole permission. A permission that is granted on '*' and never used is pure risk with no benefit.

tasks.prompt: Compare the unused-access report with processor.py (what the code actually calls). Which changes right-size the role without breaking the function? Select all that apply.
options: Remove iam:PassRole entirely: the function never passes a role to anything
Replace dynamodb:* with GetItem, PutItem and Query on the invoices table ARN, the only calls the code makes
Keep s3:* on all resources and add an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteBucket
Remove the logs permissions because they do not appear as unused
tasks.explanation: Right-sizing means granting exactly the actions and resources the code uses and dropping the rest. A Deny list on top of s3:* is fragile because every new dangerous action must be remembered, and the logging permissions are used on every invocation (they are not in the unused report), so removing them would only break observability.

tasks.prompt: The analyzer says s3:ListAllMyBuckets has been unused for 90 days. The team mentions a year-end job that sometimes lists buckets. What is the best way to treat the report?
options: As a strong signal, not a verdict: confirm with the code and owners, then remove it and let the year-end job request exactly what it needs
Delete every unused permission automatically, since the analyzer is always right
Ignore the report: unused permissions are harmless
Wait a further year before touching anything
tasks.explanation: Unused-access findings only reflect the observation window, so rare jobs can look unused. Use them to focus your review, check against the code and the owners, then cut and give the rare job its own narrowly scoped role. Auto-deleting trusts the window blindly; ignoring or waiting keeps the risk.

tasks.prompt: Rewrite invoice-processor-role's policy using the report and processor.py. It must reach only: objects under the invoices/ prefix of acme-invoices-prod (get and put), the one secret prod/invoice-api-key (get its value), the one table invoices (GetItem, PutItem, Query), and its own log group. It must not be able to pass any role.

tasks.explanation: Each wildcard statement became exact actions on exact ARNs: one prefix, one secret, one table, one log group. iam:PassRole is simply gone, so nothing in this role can be used to hand a more powerful role to another service. The 'allow' tests protect the function's real behaviour while the 'deny' tests prove the blast radius shrank.

tasks.prompt: In the terminal: review the unused-access finding, apply your rewritten policy from the editor (file://role-policy-fixed.json), confirm the function still works, then run the re-check script and paste the gate token it prints.
tasks.explanation: The change was gated on the analyzer evidence, applied, smoke-tested to prove the function still works, and re-checked clean. That sequence (evidence, change, verify) is how you cut permissions confidently instead of guessing and breaking production.

tasks.prompt: Why was iam:PassRole on Resource '*' the most dangerous statement in the original role?
options: A compromised function could hand any role in the account, including a powerful one, to a service it can drive and so act with more privilege than it was given
PassRole slows down every Lambda invocation
PassRole lets the function read any S3 object directly
PassRole is only needed for cross-account access, so it is always an error
tasks.explanation: iam:PassRole is a privilege-escalation primitive: combined with permission to create or update a resource that runs code, it lets the holder borrow another role's power. A function that never needs to pass roles should have no PassRole at all, and where it is needed it must name the role ARN and the target service.

takeaways: Right-size execution roles from evidence: the unused-access report plus the code tell you what to keep, and what to remove.
Scope every allow to exact actions and ARNs (one prefix, one secret, one table); drop iam:PassRole unless the function truly passes roles.
Treat unused-access findings as a signal to verify, then smoke-test after the change so you cut permissions without breaking the workload.
